The Scroll Container
& the minimal layout engine
How a React <Scroll> element becomes a clipped, focusable,
D-pad-scrollable viewport on a PlayStation Vita — without a layout engine,
except for the one tiny rule it ships with: stack children in a column.
↑ ↓ D-pad / arrows◀ analog stick⊙ mouse wheel✛ scissor clipping
VitaDeck renders React on a QuickJS thread and draws with raylib on the UI thread.
The two meet at a double-buffered instance tree: JS mutates a back buffer,
then swaps an immutable snapshot to the front. Scroll position deliberately
lives on neither side of that handoff — it is UI-thread state keyed by instance id,
so scrolling never round-trips through React.
<Scroll x y width height gap padding>
The SDK component emits a vita-scroll host element.
Diffs the element tree; create/update flows into flat native calls.
QuickJS binding builds an NT_SCROLL node in the back buffer.
Arena-allocated deep copy, swapped in under a mutex after each commit.
Focus, D-pad, analog stick and wheel mutate the scroll-offset map.
Column flow → scissor clip → children → scrollbar → focus ring.
⟿  scroll offsets survive the swap — the map in scroll.c is keyed by instance id,
so a re-render (new snapshot, same ids) keeps your place in the list.
Every other VitaDeck element is absolutely positioned. Scroll introduces exactly
one layout behavior — column flow — implemented in ~20 lines
participate; anything else renders at its own coordinates and is skipped by the flow.
message[0] · user
message[1] · agent
message[2] · user
message[3] · clipped ↓
viewport clips at height — BeginScissorMode()
y is a margin, not a position
A stacked child's y nudges it down from its flow slot and pushes every later sibling — exactly like margin-top.
x is relative to the padded content area, untouched by the flow. That single degree of freedom is what lets chat bubbles alternate left / right.
The flow reads height straight from props — no text measuring. That keeps hit-testing font-free and the whole engine trivially small.
flow_y  = place_y + child.height + gap
content_height = flow_y − gap + 2·padding
max_scroll     = max(0, content_height − viewport_height)
Rendering re-runs the same flow math, offsets everything by the stored scroll position,
and lets the GPU do the overflow work via raylib's scissor test. The offset is clamped
against max_scroll every frame, so content that shrinks can never strand
// src/ui/render.c — render_scroll_instance (shape of it)
BeginScissorMode(abs_x, abs_y, width, height); // ✂ overflow:hidden
content_origin = (abs_x + padding, abs_y + padding - offset);
if scroll_flow_step(child, gap, &flow_y, &base) // rect / button → stacked
render(child at content_origin) // text etc → free placement
if (focused(id)) draw_focus_ring(); // white 2px outline
Hit-testing in instance_tree.c mirrors this exactly: it walks the same flow,
subtracts the same offset, and refuses to hit children outside the viewport — so a button
scrolled out of view can't be clicked through the clip edge.
The container registers itself as a single focusable element (its children don't compete).
Once focused, it consumes up/down — navigation only wins back the D-pad
when the list is already at an edge. One press at the limit moves focus away; anywhere
held scrolls continuously while the container has focus; consumed until the edge is reached, then the next press navigates focus away.
Proportional smooth scrolling past a 25% deadzone — tilt gently for slow reading, slam it to fly.
No focus needed: instance_scroll_at(x, y) finds the deepest scroll container under the cursor and nudges it.
The Shell swapping Deck Apps calls scroll_reset() — stale offsets from the previous app's ids are dropped wholesale.
